Revisiting Gygaxs Advice on How to Have a Great AD&D Campaign

"I read stuff from the second edition days and it drives me nuts because it’s written by people that have barely played at all. The game design necessarily suffers and the game mastering advice is downright execrable as a result."

LOLWAT?

Dave Cook was anything buy a neophyte when he did 2E (for example, he did the Expert set of the infamous B/X D&D, he did Oriental Adventures for 1E, etc.).

Cook also did A1 of the slaver series. However, the gamemastering advice in the 2E DMG was slim compared to the 1E DMG.

However, to be fair, Gygax's advice appears to be for his own campaign. And it became clear early on that different people had very different ideas. That's where ideas like the Arduin Grimoire came from, etc.

Most of Gygax's ideas were sound, but his tables were either hastily put together, or not proof-read clearly; examples: look at the 1st Ed. DMG dungeon stocking table (TABLE V. F.: CHAMBER OR ROOM CONTENTS (d20) p. 171). A roll of less than 13 indicates an empty room.

Now Look at the village of Hommlet (module T-1) or B-2 Keep on the Borderlands. Are 60% of the keyed locations empty? Of course not. That table might have worked for Castle Greyhawk, but that doesn't work for most published adventures.

Now the random dungeon generator was very cool, and I used it a lot, but I stocked a lot more rooms than that chart called for.

Now look at magic swords (DMG p. 166 and a roll of 55 - the average - gives you Lawful Good... to get absolute neutral you need to roll between 61-80) which is interesting as your typical NPC is Chaotic Evil or Chaotic Neutral (DMG p. 100 roll of 5 or 6 on a d10; to get a lawful good NPC requires a roll of 1). And then there's that Sage Table (DMG p. 32) where Sages are most often Lawful Neutral...

I guess while most of society is looting and pillaging, the wise sages are trying to hold society together, while the PCs smite the unruly NPCs. Or perhaps ignore the tables unless it's convenient to use in the middle of a game session.

The one thing I took away from all of this was: use the tables, until you see a need not to use the tables or create your own tables that work better for you.
